intro: Zoe, 19, student with a part-time job. Opening: checking $600, savings $700, tuition fund $300. No debt, no crypto. Months 1 to 4: income $1,600, bills $1,500. Months 5 to 10: hours cut, income $1,300, bills $1,400. Month 8: $1,500 for the housing deposit and books. Month 12: first tuition payment of $1,500 plus a $45 plan fee; the other $3,000 is still owed afterward. The $45 plan fee and all other amounts are assumptions in this story.
plan: "Accessible bank balances" means checking + savings + tuition fund. They are accessible, not all free to spend: the tuition fund is earmarked for the month-12 payment.
Card: $800 limit, about 2% a month. If a bill is bigger than the room left on the card, the whole bill goes unpaid and a $35 late fee is added.

A DeFi yield vault is a crypto service that pays a variable rate on deposits. It is not an insured bank account, and its rate and terms here are story assumptions; real vaults differ. In this story, buying or selling costs 0.5%; sales of crypto also cost a $19 on-chain fee per holding. In this story, a sale settles within the month.
Every purchase amount includes the 0.5% fee: the full amount leaves your cash and the asset receives the amount minus the fee.

questions.title: Up to 18%
questions.situation: A classmate shows you a DeFi yield vault: a crypto service that says it pays "up to 18% a year" on money you deposit. Unlike an insured bank savings account, a vault deposit is not FDIC-insured, and an advertised top rate is not a promise. In this story, moving money in or out costs a 0.5% fee. You already know two bills are coming: $1,500 for the housing deposit in month 8, and your first tuition payment of $1,500 (plus a $45 plan fee) in month 12. The other $3,000 of tuition will still be owed after that. Your hours may also get tighter.

a.t: Keep your money in insured savings for now.

b.t: Move $300 from savings into the yield vault.

c.t: Put $400 in the yield vault and $300 in ETH (Ether, the main crypto asset of the Ethereum network), from savings.

a.text: You chose to keep your money in savings. Nothing changed. It earns 100 because money with a due date should stay where you can reach it on that date. "Up to 18%" is an advertised top rate, not a promise. Next: your savings stay available for the month-8 deposit.
a.ref: You chose to keep your money in savings. Nothing changed. It earns 100 because money with a due date should stay where you can reach it on that date. "Up to 18%" is an advertised top rate, not a promise. Next: your savings stay available for the month-8 deposit.

b.text: You moved $300 to the vault. Savings is $300 lower and the vault holds $300 minus a small fee, with a variable yield. It scores 0 because your cash did not have $300 of room above what you will owe. Next: you have $300 less bank cash for month 8, and getting it back costs a fee.
b.ref: You moved $300 to the vault. Savings is $300 lower and the vault holds $300 minus a small fee, with a variable yield. It scores 0 because your cash did not have $300 of room above what you will owe. Next: you have $300 less bank cash for month 8, and getting it back costs a fee.

c.text: You put $700 into the vault and ETH, which empties your savings. It scores 0 because that is more than your cash could spare, and half of it sits in a price that can swing. Next: the ETH shows up in Q2, and your month-8 cash is $700 lower.
c.ref: You put $700 into the vault and ETH, which empties your savings. It scores 0 because that is more than your cash could spare, and half of it sits in a price that can swing. Next: the ETH shows up in Q2, and your month-8 cash is $700 lower.

questions.takeaway: Match money to its deadline. DeFi can suit some people with spare money they can leave alone for a long time. Your tuition and deposit money is not that.

questions.title: An unexpected message about aid
questions.situation: You get an email that says it is from your school. It says you may be selected for a $1,000 award, asks you to connect your crypto wallet to "claim" it, and mentions a $40 processing fee. You did not apply for anything like this.

a.t: Don't pay or connect anything. Look up the school's financial aid office yourself and ask them.

c.t: Connect your wallet to see what it asks.

a.text: You checked through the school's own office instead of the message. Nothing was lost. It earns 100 because you cannot tell from the message whether it is real, and the safe move is to confirm through a source you found yourself. If an award is real, the aid office can tell you the proper way to receive it. Next: your cash and wallet are unchanged.
a.ref: You checked through the school's own office instead of the message. Nothing was lost. It earns 100 because you cannot tell from the message whether it is real, and the safe move is to confirm through a source you found yourself. If an award is real, the aid office can tell you the proper way to receive it. Next: your cash and wallet are unchanged.

b.text: You paid $40. It is gone and no award appeared. It scores 0 because you paid an unverified stranger for a promise. Next: you have $40 less for month 8.
b.ref: You paid $40. It is gone and no award appeared. It scores 0 because you paid an unverified stranger for a promise. Next: you have $40 less for month 8.

c.text: You connected your wallet and approved a request. The wallet was emptied: all your ETH, or $120 of cash if you had none. It scores 0 because connecting and approving can let someone else move your funds. Next: you have less to work with in month 8.
c.ref: You connected your wallet and approved a request. The wallet was emptied: all your ETH, or $120 of cash if you had none. It scores 0 because connecting and approving can let someone else move your funds. Next: you have less to work with in month 8.

questions.takeaway: Verify unexpected requests independently before paying, signing or connecting anything. Never share a recovery phrase. This does not mean real aid asks for these things; the point is that you cannot tell from the message.

questions.takeaway: A 100 means the best choice at that moment, not that every bill was paid. Compare the full cost: fees, interest and what is left unpaid. Fees can swamp small transfers: in this story, moving $25 on-chain can cost $19. A card advance is borrowing, not cash. Real card advances usually add a fee and a higher rate; this story uses one simple rate of about 2% a month. Never describe an unpaid bill as paid.
